s: In the Gade Sai Krishna custodial-death case, the NHRC directed which combination of authorities to submit a report?
o: The Union Home Ministry, DGP and District Collector
The State Election Commission, DGP and Chief Justice of the High Court
The Governor, Speaker and Advocate-General of Andhra Pradesh
The Andhra Pradesh SHRC, DGP and Chief Secretary
x: In the Gade Sai Krishna case, the NHRC directed the Andhra Pradesh SHRC, the Director General of Police and the Chief Secretary to report.

s: After bifurcation, which city was notified as the headquarters of the Andhra Pradesh SHRC?
x: Kurnool was notified as the AP SHRC headquarters (earlier planned at Vijayawada); the office opened in September 2021.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Andhra Pradesh SHRC:
1. It was constituted by the AP Government under the PHRA, 1993.
2. Its office at Kurnool was inaugurated in September 2021.
3. It has had a full-time chairperson continuously since 2021.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct; statement 3 is wrong because the AP SHRC has reportedly been without a chairperson since March 2024.

s: Who was the Chairperson of the Andhra Pradesh State Human Rights Commission when its Kurnool office was inaugurated in 2021?
x: Justice M. Seetharama Murti, a retired High Court judge, was the AP SHRC Chairperson when the Kurnool office opened in September 2021.

s: Under which of the following was the National Human Rights Commission set up as a statutory body?
x: The NHRC is a statutory body under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, set up in conformity with the Paris Principles; it is not a constitutional body.

s: What kind of body is the National Human Rights Commission of India?
o: Executive body set up by Cabinet resolution
x: The NHRC is statutory, not constitutional, because it was created by the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.

s: By which of the following was the National Human Rights Commission created as a statutory body?
o: The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993
x: The NHRC is a statutory body created under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993; it is not a constitutional body.

s: To which of the following does the establishment of the NHRC conform?
x: The NHRC was established in conformity with the Paris Principles relating to national institutions for the promotion and protection of human rights.

s: Who was the first Chairperson of the National Human Rights Commission?
x: Justice Ranganath Misra was the first Chairperson of the NHRC, constituted on 12 October 1993.

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Paris Principles?
o: They prescribe the procedure for prosecuting custodial deaths before Human Rights Courts.
They prescribe standards of independence, pluralism and a broad mandate for national human-rights institutions.
They establish the jurisdiction of State Human Rights Commissions over Union Territories.
They classify national human-rights institutions as A or B categories.
x: The Paris Principles, adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1993, set standards of independence, pluralism and a broad mandate for national human-rights institutions.

s: Which of the following is a statutory body and not a constitutional body?
x: The NHRC is statutory (PHRA 1993); UPSC and CAG are constitutional bodies, and the NCBC got constitutional status by the 102nd Amendment (2018).

s: Who is the present Chairperson of the NHRC (as of February 2026)?
x: Justice V. Ramasubramanian is the present NHRC Chairperson; Justice Ranganath Misra was the first.

s: On which date was the Protection of Human Rights Ordinance, from which the Act is deemed in force, issued?
x: The ordinance came on 28 September 1993; the NHRC was constituted on 12 October 1993 and the Act got assent in January 1994.

s: In which year was the National Human Rights Commission constituted?
x: The NHRC was constituted on 12 October 1993; the Act only got assent in January 1994, so '1994' is a trap.

s:
Consider the following statements about the National Human Rights Commission:
1. It is a constitutional body.
2. It was constituted on 12 October 1993.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The NHRC is a statutory body under the PHRA, 1993, not a constitutional one; it was constituted on 12 October 1993.

s: When did the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 receive the President's assent?
x: The ordinance came on 28 September 1993 and the NHRC was constituted on 12 October 1993; the Act got assent in January 1994.

s: The Chairperson of the National Commission for Backward Classes is a deemed member of the NHRC. By which Constitutional Amendment did the NCBC get constitutional status?
x: The NCBC, set up by an Act in 1993, got constitutional status by the 102nd Amendment (2018).

s: Under the Act, 'human rights' are rights relating to life, liberty, equality and what else?
x: Human rights means rights relating to life, liberty, equality and dignity guaranteed by the Constitution or International Covenants and enforceable by Indian courts.

s: After the 2019 amendment, who besides a former Chief Justice of India can be the NHRC Chairperson?
o: Chief Justice of a High Court
x: The 2019 amendment allows a former CJI or a Supreme Court judge to chair the NHRC; any HC judge is eligible only for the SHRC chair.

s: Which of the following was added as a deemed member of the NHRC by the 2019 amendment?
x: The 2019 amendment added the chairs of the NCBC and NCPCR and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities as deemed members.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the deemed members of the NHRC after the 2019 amendment?
o: There are now seven deemed members.
The NCBC Chairperson was added in 2019.
The Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities was added in 2019.
The NCPCR Chairperson was a deemed member even before 2019.
x: The NCPCR Chairperson was one of the three heads added in 2019 to the four earlier deemed members, making seven.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the composition of the NHRC?
o: It includes one former or serving Judge of the Supreme Court.
At least one woman must be among its human-rights experts.
It includes one former or serving Chief Justice or Judge of a High Court.
It includes two persons having knowledge of human rights.
x: The NHRC includes three persons with knowledge of human rights, at least one of whom must be a woman.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about deemed members of the NHRC?
o: The NCSC and NCST Chairpersons became deemed members through the 2006 amendment.
Only the Chairpersons of the commissions concerned are deemed members.
A deemed member is identical in status to an ordinary NHRC member.
The NCBC Chairperson was added as a deemed member in 2019.
x: The deemed-member provision does not convert the Chairpersons into ordinary NHRC members.

s: Since the 2019 amendment, besides a former Chief Justice of India, who is eligible to be NHRC Chairperson?
o: A Judge of the Supreme Court
A former Chief Justice of a High Court
x: Before 2019 only a former CJI could be Chairperson; the 2019 amendment also made a Supreme Court Judge eligible.

s: The Secretary-General of the NHRC exercises which powers under the Chairperson's control?
x: The Secretary-General has administrative and financial powers, not judicial ones.

s: Which deemed member of the NHRC is NOT the chairperson of a national commission?
o: Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities
Chairperson, National Commission for Backward Classes
x: The Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities is the only deemed member who is not a commission chair.

s: Who can be appointed Chairperson of a State Human Rights Commission after the 2019 amendment?
o: Only a former Chief Justice of a High Court
A former Chief Justice or Judge of a High Court
Only a former Judge of the Supreme Court
Any District Judge with seven years' service
x: Since 2019 a former High Court Judge, not only a former High Court Chief Justice, can chair an SHRC.

s: Which amendment made the Chairpersons of the National Commissions for SCs and STs deemed members of the NHRC?
x: The NCSC and NCST chairs became deemed members in 2006; three more were added in 2019.

s: To how many did the 2019 amendment raise the NHRC's human-rights expert members from two?
o: Three, at least one a woman
Five, at least one a woman
x: Since 2019 there are three human-rights experts, at least one of them a woman (earlier two).

s: A sitting Judge of the Supreme Court or a sitting Chief Justice of a High Court can be appointed to the NHRC only after consultation with whom?
x: Appointment of a sitting Supreme Court Judge or a sitting High Court Chief Justice requires consultation with the Chief Justice of India.

s: A member of the NHRC submits a written resignation during the tenure of office. To whom should it be addressed?
x: A Chairperson or member of the NHRC resigns by writing addressed to the President of India.

s: For removal of the NHRC Chairperson on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity, to whom does the President refer the matter?
x: The President refers such cases to the Supreme Court for inquiry; grounds like insolvency allow direct removal by the President.

s: After demitting office, what is the position of the Chairperson or a member of the NHRC regarding further employment?
o: eligible for employment under either the Central or State Government without restriction
ineligible for further employment under the Central or any State Government
eligible for any post under the Central Government but not under a State Government
eligible only for judicial employment under the Central Government
x: The Chairperson and members are not eligible for further employment under the Central Government or any State Government after leaving office.

s: The Chairperson and members of the NHRC are appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee headed by the Prime Minister. Which one of the following is NOT a member of that committee?
o: Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
x: The six-member committee is the Prime Minister (chair), Speaker of the Lok Sabha, Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, Leaders of Opposition in both Houses and the Union Home Minister. The Chief Justice of India is not a member; he is only consulted before a sitting SC Judge or HC Chief Justice is appointed.

s: Which office-holder of the Rajya Sabha is a member of the NHRC selection committee besides its Leader of Opposition?
x: The Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha sits on the six-member PM-led committee; the Chairman (Vice-President) does not.

s: Under the Protection of Human Rights (Amendment) Act, 2019, what is the position on reappointment of NHRC members?
o: is limited to the Chairperson for one further term
is barred after the first term
is permitted, the earlier five-year limit having been removed
needs a compulsory gap of five years
x: The 2019 amendment removed the earlier five-year limit, so members remain eligible for reappointment, subject to the 3-year/70 term.

s: The NHRC selection committee under Section 4 has how many members?
x: The Section 4 committee has six members, headed by the Prime Minister.

s: Who appoints the Chairperson and members of the National Human Rights Commission?
x: The President appoints them on the advice of a six-member committee headed by the Prime Minister.

s:
Consider the following statements about the removal of the NHRC Chairperson:
1. The President can remove the Chairperson directly if he is adjudged an insolvent.
2. Removal for proved misbehaviour or incapacity needs an inquiry by the Supreme Court on the President's reference.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Insolvency, paid outside employment, infirmity, unsound mind and moral-turpitude conviction allow direct removal; misbehaviour or incapacity needs a Supreme Court inquiry.

s: Which of the following is NOT a ground on which the President may remove the Chairperson of the NHRC?
o: Engaging in paid employment outside the duties of office
Conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude
Being of unsound mind as declared by a competent court
Disagreeing with the policies of the Union Government
x: The Act lists insolvency, paid outside employment, infirmity, unsound mind, moral-turpitude conviction, and proved misbehaviour or incapacity; policy disagreement is not a ground.

s: During an inquiry, for which purpose does a Human Rights Commission have the powers of a civil court under the CPC, 1908?
o: Reviewing judgments of the High Courts
Awarding imprisonment to guilty public servants
x: The Commission has civil-court powers such as summons, requiring documents, receiving affidavits and requisitioning public records; it has no sentencing powers.

s: The Supreme Court entrusted the NHRC with monitoring the implementation of which law in 1997?
o: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
x: In 1997, the Supreme Court entrusted the NHRC with monitoring the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976.

s: With whose approval can the NHRC intervene in court proceedings involving human-rights allegations?
x: It needs the approval of the court concerned, not the Central Government.

s: Which of the following is a power of the NHRC?
o: Visiting jails to study inmates' living conditions
Unrestricted investigation of the armed forces
x: The NHRC may visit jails and has civil-court powers, but its recommendations are advisory and it cannot directly investigate the armed forces.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about how the NHRC may take up an inquiry?
o: It may take suo motu cognisance.
It may inquire into a complaint solely against a private individual with no public servant involved.
It may act on a petition presented to it.
It may act on a direction of a court.
x: The NHRC's jurisdiction concerns violations or negligence by public servants, so a purely private complaint is outside it.

s: While inquiring into complaints, the NHRC has the powers of which court?
x: The NHRC has civil-court powers such as summoning persons, examining them on oath, requiring documents and requisitioning public records.

s: Which of the following can the National Human Rights Commission do with respect to relief?
o: Grant relief only after a criminal court records conviction
Recommend compensation and interim relief, including during the inquiry
Punish the public servant and recover the amount directly
Award final compensation in every case without recommendation
x: The NHRC may recommend compensation, prosecution and interim relief. Since the 2006 amendment, it may recommend interim relief even during the inquiry.

s: What is the nature of the recommendations of the NHRC?
o: Binding decrees of a civil court
A source of automatic criminal liability
Advisory, though the Government must inform it of action taken
x: NHRC recommendations are advisory and cannot be compelled; the Government must only inform the Commission of the action taken.

s: Since 2006, on what condition may the NHRC visit jails and detention centres?
x: The 2006 amendment let the NHRC visit jails without intimating the State Government.

s: In which case did the Supreme Court lay down 16-point guidelines on encounter deaths in 2014?
o: D.K. Basu v State of West Bengal
Prakash Singh v Union of India
Nilabati Behera v State of Orissa
x: PUCL v State of Maharashtra (2014) set 16-point guidelines on encounter deaths, used with NHRC reporting norms.

s: The NHRC's Advisory 2.0 issued in May 2026 concerns the welfare of which group?
x: Advisory 2.0 (May 2026) is on transgender welfare: Census categories, legal-aid cells and Garima Greh expansion.

s: Which of the following is a function of the NHRC under Section 12 of the Protection of Human Rights Act?
o: Reviewing factors, including acts of terrorism, that inhibit the enjoyment of human rights
Punishing public servants found guilty of violations
Appointing the Chairpersons of State Human Rights Commissions
Framing laws on human rights for Parliament
x: Section 12 lets the NHRC review safeguards and factors such as terrorism that inhibit human rights; it cannot punish or legislate.

s: After the NHRC sends its inquiry report with recommendations, within what period must the Government concerned inform the Commission of the action taken?
x: The Government must inform the Commission of the action taken on its report within one month. Three months is the period for the Central Government to report action in armed-forces cases; six months and one year are not the prescribed periods (one year is the time bar for inquiry).

s: Under which Section of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 are Human Rights Courts provided for?
x: Section 30 deals with Human Rights Courts; Section 31 covers Special Public Prosecutors, Section 3 the NHRC and Section 21 the SHRC.

s: To how many years did the 2019 amendment reduce the term of the NHRC Chairperson and members from 5 years?
x: The term was cut from 5 to 3 years (or age 70), and reappointment is allowed.

s:
Consider the following statements about the 2019 amendment to the PHRA:
1. Human-rights members of the NHRC rose from 2 to 3, one being a woman.
2. Any High Court judge can now chair an SHRC.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: members rose from 2 to 3 including a woman, and an SHRC chair can now be any HC judge as well.

s: What did the 2006 amendment to the Protection of Human Rights Act enable the NHRC to do?
o: Convert every district court into a Human Rights Court
Transfer all NHRC members to State service
Transfer complaints to the concerned SHRC
x: The 2006 amendment enabled the NHRC to transfer complaints to the concerned State Human Rights Commission.

s: With whose concurrence does the State Government notify Human Rights Courts under Section 30?
o: Chief Justice of the High Court
x: The State Government, with the HC Chief Justice's concurrence, notifies a Court of Session in each district as a Human Rights Court.

s: For at least how many years must a Special Public Prosecutor for a Human Rights Court (Section 31) have practised as an advocate?
x: Section 31 requires an advocate of seven years' practice.

s: Which of the following was NOT a change made by the 2006 amendment?
o: Jail visits without intimating the State Government
Reducing the term of NHRC members to three years
Transfer of complaints to the SHRC concerned
x: The term was cut from five to three years (or 70) by the 2019 amendment, not in 2006.

s: Before which body is the annual report of the NHRC laid, with a memorandum of action taken?
x: The NHRC report goes to the Central Government and is laid before each House of Parliament.

s: Under GANHRI accreditation, what does 'A' status mean for a national human rights institution?
o: Partly compliant with the Paris Principles
Fully compliant with the Paris Principles
x: GANHRI's Sub-Committee on Accreditation gives 'A' for full and 'B' for partial compliance with the Paris Principles.

s:
Consider the following statements about NHRC-India and GANHRI:
1. In May 2024 GANHRI deferred NHRC-India's re-accreditation for the second year in a row.
2. The deferral cited the NHRC's independence from government.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: GANHRI deferred re-accreditation in 2023 and again in May 2024, citing independence from government; the NHRC says its 'A' status continues.

s: What is the nature of the advice of the National Human Rights Commission to the Government?
o: Binding on both Union and States
x: NHRC advice is non-binding on the Government; the NHRC is a statutory body.

s: Under the statutory procedure concerning the armed forces, what does the NHRC do?
o: It calls for an independent report from the Central Government and makes recommendations based on that report
It transfers every complaint to the SHRC for investigation
It directly imposes criminal sentencing on members of the armed forces
It directly investigates all complaints without restriction
x: For the armed forces, the NHRC cannot investigate directly. It asks the Central Government for a report and makes recommendations on it.

s: The NHRC cannot inquire into a matter after how long from the date of the alleged act?
x: The NHRC is barred after one year from the alleged act; a review committee wanted this relaxed where sufficient cause exists.

s: Why is the NHRC criticised as a 'toothless tiger'?
o: It lacks civil-court powers during inquiries
It is not a statutory body
x: The criticism rests on its non-binding advice, along with the one-year bar and limits on armed-forces complaints.

s: In cases concerning the armed forces, within what period must the Central Government inform the NHRC of the action taken?
x: In armed-forces cases, the Central Government must inform the NHRC of the action taken within three months.
